column1: 217|A transition element is an element whose atom has an incomplete d subshell or which forms at least one common cation with an incomplete d subshell.
218|General d-block configuration: (n−1)d¹–¹⁰ ns⁰–²; exceptions occur because the d and s subshell energies are close.
219|Zn, Cd and Hg atoms and their common M²⁺ ions have filled d¹⁰ subshells, not partially filled d subshells; they therefore fail the strict transition-element definition.
220|The ns and (n−1)d orbital energies are close, so different numbers of these electrons can participate in bonding or be removed, giving multiple oxidation states.
221|The two outer ns electrons are usually lost first, giving M²⁺. The (n−1)d electrons are more tightly held, so +2 is common for first-row metals.
222|Partly filled d subshells have split d-orbital energy levels in a ligand field. Absorption of visible light promotes d–d transitions; remaining transmitted/reflected light gives colour.
223|Ligand fields split the metal d orbitals. A photon with energy matching the splitting promotes an electron between them; selective visible absorption determines observed colour.
224|A d⁰ ion has no d electron to excite and a d¹⁰ ion has no vacant d state within the split d set; thus d–d transitions are unavailable. Charge-transfer bands can still colour some compounds.
225|Changing oxidation state changes d-electron count and splitting; changing ligand alters the ligand-field strength and Δ. Both change transition energies and the wavelengths absorbed.
226|Transition metals can access multiple oxidation states, adsorb reactants on surfaces and form intermediates, providing alternative pathways with lower activation barriers.
227|Variable oxidation states allow electron transfer between reactants and metal centres. Adsorption brings reactants together and weakens bonds at the surface, lowering activation barriers.
228|Unpaired d electrons have magnetic moments; their alignment with an applied field causes paramagnetism. Ions with all electrons paired are diamagnetic.
229|Spin-only moment μ=√[n(n+2)] BM. For n=3, μ=√15=3.87 BM.
230|Many transition metals have similar atomic sizes and crystal structures, so atoms can replace one another in metallic lattices to form substitutional alloys.
231|Interstitial compounds form when small atoms such as H, C or N occupy holes in a metal lattice. They are often hard/high-melting and may be non-stoichiometric.
232|Small atoms fit into metal-lattice interstices and strongly distort/strengthen the lattice, restricting metal-atom motion; this often gives high hardness and melting points.

233|Across the first transition series, atomic radii decrease modestly at first, vary little through the middle, and may rise slightly near the end; added d electrons partly shield increasing nuclear charge.
234|Increasing nuclear charge, imperfect d-electron shielding, electron–electron repulsion and irregular stability of d configurations compete, producing a non-smooth ionisation-enthalpy trend.
235|Lanthanoid contraction is the gradual decrease in atomic and especially Ln³⁺ ionic radii from La to Lu as nuclear charge increases across the series.
236|Added 4f electrons shield the increasing nuclear charge poorly. Effective nuclear charge therefore rises across the series and contracts the electron cloud.

237|Lanthanoid contraction makes Zr and Hf nearly equal in size, so they have very similar chemistry and are difficult to separate; it also affects hydroxide basicity and other size-dependent properties.
238|The 4f electrons inserted between La and Lu shield poorly, causing lanthanoid contraction. Consequently Hf, after the lanthanoids, has almost the same radius as Zr above it.
239|General lanthanoid configuration: [Xe]4f⁰–¹⁴5d⁰–¹6s²; most Ln atoms have 4f electrons, with limited 5d participation.
240|Lanthanoids readily lose two 6s electrons and one 4f/5d electron to form Ln³⁺. This oxidation state is common because the resulting ions are generally stable in compounds.
241|+2 or +4 can provide especially stable empty, half-filled or filled 4f subshells, e.g. Ce⁴⁺ (4f⁰), Eu²⁺ (4f⁷), Tb⁴⁺ (4f⁷), Yb²⁺ (4f¹⁴); their stability also depends on lattice/hydration energies.
242|General actinoid configuration: [Rn]5f⁰–¹⁴6d⁰–²7s², with substantial variation among elements.
243|Actinoid 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are closer in energy and 5f electrons are more available for bonding than 4f electrons in lanthanoids; several electron counts can therefore participate.

244|Actinoids fill 5f orbitals whereas lanthanoids fill 4f; actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states and are all radioactive, while many lanthanoids have stable isotopes and predominantly +3 chemistry.

245|Actinoids have very heavy nuclei with large proton–proton repulsion; their nuclei are unstable and undergo radioactive decay toward more stable configurations. All actinoids are radioactive, though half-lives vary greatly.
246|Aqueous potassium dichromate is orange; chromium is in oxidation state +6.
247|Permanganate ion MnO₄⁻ is deep purple/violet in aqueous solution.
248|Cr₂O₇²⁻+14H⁺+6e⁻→2Cr³⁺+7H₂O.
249|MnO₄⁻+8H⁺+5e⁻→Mn²⁺+4H₂O.
250|Acidified KMnO₄ accepts electrons and oxidises many reductants (e.g. Fe²⁺→Fe³⁺ or I⁻→I₂); MnO₄⁻ is reduced mainly to pale Mn²⁺ in sufficiently acidic solution.

251|H⁺ participates in the reduction half-reaction, so its concentration shifts the redox equilibrium and changes the reduction potential/products. Acid favours Mn²⁺; neutral/weakly alkaline conditions commonly yield MnO₂; strongly alkaline conditions can yield MnO₄²⁻.
252|In K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1)+2x+7(−2)=0, so x=+6 for chromium.
253|In KMnO₄: (+1)+x+4(−2)=0, so manganese is +7.
254|For MnO₄²⁻, x+4(−2)=−2, so Mn=+6. In MnO₄⁻, Mn=+7; manganate is one oxidation state lower.

255|Cr²⁺ (d⁴) readily loses an electron to form particularly stable Cr³⁺ (d³), so it reduces other species. Mn³⁺ (d⁴) readily gains an electron to form half-filled Mn²⁺ (d⁵), so it can oxidise other species.
256|Cr³⁺ is d³, with a stable t₂g³ arrangement in an octahedral field; Mn²⁺ is d⁵ and gains half-filled-subshell stability. Their stability also depends on environment and hydration.
257|Several d and s electrons can contribute to metal–metal bonding; strong cohesive bonding requires substantial energy to separate atoms, giving high atomisation enthalpies.

258|Melting points generally rise toward the middle of the first transition series, where metallic bonding is strong, then fall toward the end as d participation/cohesion declines. Subshell configurations, structure and bonding make the trend irregular.
259|Disproportionation is simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same oxidation state, e.g. 2Cu⁺(aq)→Cu²⁺(aq)+Cu(s).
260|In water, Cu²⁺ is strongly stabilised by hydration relative to Cu⁺; the free-energy balance makes 2Cu⁺→Cu²⁺+Cu favourable under standard aqueous conditions.
261|Many transition-metal ions have partly filled d levels with ligand-field or charge-transfer absorptions in visible light; selective absorption produces vivid colours useful in pigments.
262|High-spin d⁵ has five unpaired electrons, μ=√35=5.92 BM, and is strongly paramagnetic. Low-spin d⁶ has t₂g⁶, no unpaired electrons, μ≈0, and is diamagnetic (octahedral spin-only model).

263|Lanthanoid contraction is due to increasing nuclear charge poorly shielded by 4f electrons; actinoid contraction arises similarly from poor 5f shielding. Both shrink trivalent ionic radii across their series; actinoid behaviour is less regular because 5f participation is greater.

264|Ln³⁺ ions have similar charge and only gradually changing radii/chemistry, making their separation difficult. The small systematic contraction does produce gradual differences in basicity, complexation and related properties that can be exploited.
265|Chromium has 3d and 4s valence electrons available, and strongly electronegative oxygen stabilises high oxidation state +6 in chromate/dichromate oxyanions.
266|2CrO₄²⁻+2H⁺⇌Cr₂O₇²⁻+H₂O. Acid shifts yellow chromate toward orange dichromate; added base removes H⁺ and shifts back toward chromate.
267|Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ rather than 3d⁴4s². The 3d and 4s energies are close, and the half-filled d⁵ subshell provides extra stability.
268|Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ rather than the simple expected distributions; near-degenerate 4s/3d levels allow configurations with half-filled or filled d subshells.
269|Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, a particularly stable half-filled configuration. Removing a third electron breaks that arrangement, so the third ionisation enthalpy is relatively high.
270|Fe²⁺ is d⁶; Fe³⁺ is d⁵, a half-filled subshell, which often favours Fe³⁺. Relative stability is environment-dependent because hydration, lattice energy and ligand fields also contribute.
271|Sc commonly forms Sc³⁺ by losing its two 4s and one 3d electron, leaving the stable [Ar] configuration.

272|Early transition metals have fewer d electrons and can use more valence electrons in bonding, making high oxidation states more accessible. Later metals have higher ionisation costs and increasingly stable lower d configurations.
273|Transition-metal ions are often small with high charge density and vacant/available orbitals; they can accept ligand lone pairs and form coordinate bonds.

274|The number and arrangement of unpaired d electrons determine spin-only moment μ=√[n(n+2)] BM. Any unpaired electrons give paramagnetism; all paired gives diamagnetism; ligand strength can change pairing in complexes.
275|Cu²⁺ is d⁹ with a partially filled d level, allowing visible d–d transitions. Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰ with no d–d transition and is usually colourless unless charge-transfer absorption occurs.
276|Ligand identity sets ligand-field strength through its bonding and interaction with metal d orbitals, changing Δ. The absorbed photon energy and d–d transition wavelength therefore change.
277|Basicity of lanthanoid hydroxides generally decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃ as Ln³⁺ radius contracts and polarising power/covalent character increase.
278|Across La to Lu, Ln³⁺ size decreases while charge remains +3. Greater polarisation strengthens Ln–O covalent character and reduces hydroxide basicity; La(OH)₃ is more basic than Lu(OH)₃.

279|Actinoid 5f orbitals are more spatially extended and can participate in bonding, and actinoids commonly access higher oxidation states and strong metal–ligand interactions; this favours complex formation.

280|The 5f, 6d and 7s levels are close in energy, so several configurations and oxidation states are accessible. This, plus greater 5f bonding participation and radioactivity, makes actinoid chemistry complex.
281|Chromite ore is oxidised/roasted to soluble chromate. H₂SO₄ acidifies the chromate solution, shifting 2CrO₄²⁻+2H⁺⇌Cr₂O₇²⁻+H₂O toward dichromate; adding KCl then crystallises less-soluble K₂Cr₂O₇.
282|MnO₄⁻+5Fe²⁺+8H⁺→Mn²⁺+5Fe³⁺+4H₂O.
283|In acid, H⁺ drives the MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺ reduction half-reaction, whose potential is more positive; permanganate is consequently a stronger oxidant than when reduced to MnO₂ in neutral medium.
284|K₂Cr₂O₇ is available in high purity, stable in air, non-hygroscopic, has a relatively high molar mass and can be weighed accurately to prepare a standard solution.
285|Delocalised mobile electrons carry charge and transport thermal energy through the metallic lattice, giving transition metals generally good electrical and thermal conductivity.
286|Zn and Cd have filled (n−1)d¹⁰ subshells and fewer unpaired d electrons to strengthen metal–metal cohesion; their metallic bonding and atomisation enthalpies are comparatively lower.
287|Transition metals involve filling d orbitals in the outer transition series; inner-transition metals involve progressive filling of inner f orbitals (lanthanoids 4f, actinoids 5f).

288|E° reflects several energetic terms—atomisation, ionisation, hydration/solvation and entropy—not just the electron configuration. Their balance depends on the species and medium, so configuration alone is insufficient.
